Chapter 5. The Web of Lies and the Making of Legends.
Think about it—every culture has its own legends. Stories that somehow get a little bigger with each telling, shaped by what people need, or what they're afraid of, right in that moment. Sometimes, those legends start out as tiny lies—little distortions that, over time, become accepted as just the way things are. Other times, the lies are intentional, spun to protect a secret, or maybe to shield someone who can’t defend themselves.
In comics, just like in real life, that line between what’s true and what’s made up? It’s almost never as clear as we’d like.
As Superman’s fame skyrocketed, the story about how he came to be turned into a legend of its own. Fans argued about his origins, trying to find hidden meaning in every little detail. Was Superman really a symbol of what it’s like to be an immigrant? Or was he a modern-day Moses, sent to save us? The real answer? It’s a lot messier than any single theory.
The truth is, Superman sprang from a mix of personal pain, cultural myth, and sheer creative ambition.
But behind all that, the creators themselves were fighting their own battles. There were contracts, rights sold off, fortunes made—but not by the guys who actually dreamed up the Man of Steel. The story of Superman’s creation ended up as a warning about the price of genius, and just how much power big companies have when it comes to shaping what we remember.
The real people behind Superman? More often than not, they were pushed into the background, their struggles hidden behind the hero’s bright red cape.
And then, there’s the shadow that never quite faded—the unsolved murder of Mitchell Siegel. It’s one of those mysteries you just can’t tie up with a neat little bow. People searched for answers, but mostly found dead ends and half-truths. Still, every now and then, there were moments of surprising connection.
The story of a father’s death and a son’s incredible creation wove together in ways nobody could’ve seen coming.
Most of us never really notice just how much of our world is built from stories. Some are true. Some are made up. But all of them? They’re powerful. The lies we tell, the secrets we keep, and the legends we build—they’re not just distractions.
They’re the bricks and mortar of culture itself. They give us a way to make sense of chaos and loss, to find meaning when things feel out of control.
